earlier_scan.source_named: Glottolog yang1288 lists only Merlan 1994 subclassification comment; no descriptive grammar of Yangman located (language dormant)

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.x languoid record yang1288 Yangman and family yang1287 Yangmanic (JSON).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Bibliographic only: Glottolog's most extensive description = wordlist or less (Capell 1956 ms 600-word vocabulary; Elkin 1953-56); links to AUSTLANG N68, ELP 5986, PHOIBLE.

sources.citation: StressTyp2 SQL dump (StressTyp2-v1-archive-0415) and WALS/StressTyp2 language tables held by the project.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Yangman [jng] appears only in the ISO code table; no lect/passage for Yangman. Wardaman the StressTyp2 entry for this language carries the Merlan 1994:53-54 penult paragraph.

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: No stress statement; says 'Dagoman and Yangman were either dialects or closely related languages; as a family, these are called Yangmanic' (citing Merlan 1994, Dixon 2002:xl).

sources.citation: Evans, Nicholas (ed.). 2003. The non-Pama-Nyungan languages of northern Australia: comparative studies of the continent's most linguistically complex region (Pacific Linguistics 552). Canberra: ANU.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing for Yangman; p.14 only classifies 'Wagiman, and Wardaman/Dagoman/Yangman' as provisionally excised from Gunwinyguan. Harvey's Proto-Gunwinyguan phonology chapter cites Wardaman segmental facts only.

sources.citation: Capell, Arthur. 1979. Classification of verbs in Australian languages. In S. A. Wurm (ed.), Australian Linguistic Studies, 229-322 (Pacific Linguistics C-54). Canberra: ANU.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on stress placement. p.247-248: Yangman 'noted by Capell but no material on them has yet been published'. p.249: 'Yangman is one of the few Australian languages that show a strong tonal patterning: here it is wógbà ŋānímēn' with fn.1 'an acute accent indicates high tone, grave the low tone, and macron the mid or level tone.' Passing prosodic remark from Capell's 1940s field notes; only first-hand statement about Yangman prosody located.

sources.citation: Kinslow-Harris, Joy. 1969. Descriptive and comparative study of the Gunwingguan languages, Northern Territory. PhD thesis, Australian National University (hdl 1885/132713).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Stress section ('STRESS AND INTONATION', primary stress initial / penult in multi-root words) describes Gunwinggu only; Yangman ('Jungman', 'Jangman') appears only in the classification list (Yangmanic Group: Nolgin subgroup Jungman, Yibiwan subgroup Wardaman) and in ceremonial-relations prose. Nothing on Yangman stress.

sources.citation: PHOIBLE 2.0, inventory ER 3016 'Yangman' (contributor Erich Round), source record merlan_grammar_1994 = Merlan, A Grammar of Wardaman (MGL 11).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Segment inventory only (17 consonants incl. t ʈ ȶ k p.., vowels); no suprasegmental information; shows the Yangman inventory is extracted from Merlan's Wardaman grammar.

sources.citation: The Rosetta Project. n.d. Yangman Swadesh List (archive.org rosettaproject_jng_swadesh-1).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Wordlist only, no prose; one form carries an acute (maŋunínan 'bitter') of unstated meaning.

sources.citation: Merlan, Francesca C. 1994. A Grammar of Wardaman: a language of the Northern Territory of Australia (Mouton Grammar Library 11). Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter. Ch.1 'Close linguistic relationships' pp.2-4 (DOI 10.1515/9783110871371.1) and Ch.3 'Process phonology' stress pp.53-56 (DOI 10.1515/9783110871371.25).
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.access_detail: a digital copy exists, paywalled at the publisher (DOI); library e-access not checked
sources.note: Only modern description in Yangmanic; pp.2-4 state how Yangman and Dagoman relate to Wardaman (dialect vs language, shared phonology) and pp.53-56 give the penultimate-stress rule; needed to decide whether the Wardaman rule can be cited for yang1288 and whether Merlan says anything Yangman-specific about prosody.

sources.citation: Capell, Arthur. 1940. The classification of languages in north and north-west Australia. Oceania 10(3): 241-272; 10(4): 404-433.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.note: Capell's areal survey covering the Katherine-region prefixing languages (Wardaman group); may contain a line on accent for the group, though Capell 1979:247-248 says no Yangman material had been published.

sources.citation: Capell, Arthur. c.1940s. Yangman ('Jangman') field notes and the ms 'A vocabulary of 600 words in forty North Australian languages' (1956), language 34 Jangman; Capell papers, PARADISEC collections AC1/AC2.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.note: Capell 1979:249 quotes these notes with tone/stress diacritics ('strong tonal patterning'); the notes may carry accent marks on the wordlist from which a stress position could be read, and are the only other first-hand Yangman data.

sources.citation: Merlan, Francesca. 1970s-1990s. Yangman and Dagoman field notes, elicitation and recordings with last speakers (unpublished; AIATSIS / possibly PARADISEC deposits; basis of the Yangman remarks in Merlan 1994).
